questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value
questions.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,2$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
18,\,12,\,8,\,\frac{16}{3},\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=18$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{12}{18}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =18{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,2.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,2 \\ 18{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} & <0.000\,2 \\ {(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.000\,2}{18} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})}+1≈29.159
$$

Therefore, the $30$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,2.$

$$

The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=64$ and the common ratio is

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.001 \\ 64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <0.001 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.001}{64} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1≈39.386
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown
questions.problem:
The $3$rd term of a geometric sequence is $75$, and the common ratio is $5.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$1\,713?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{3}=75$ and  $r=5$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {5}^{3-1} \\ 75 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {5}^{2} \\ 75 & =25{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {5}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $1\,713.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot {5}^{n-1} & >1\,713 \\ {5}^{n-1} & >571 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{5}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(571) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(5) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(571) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(571)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(571)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(571)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}+1≈4.944
$$

Therefore, the $5$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\,713.$

questions.problem: The $5$th term of a geometric sequence is $81$, and the common ratio is $\frac{3}{2}.$ The first term of this sequence to exceed $10\,000$ is the{{field-1}} th term.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{5}=81$ and  $r=\frac{3}{2}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{5} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{5-1} \\ 81 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{4} \\ 81 & =\frac{81}{16}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =16\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $10\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}16\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >10\,000 \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >625 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(625) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(625) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(625)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(625)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(625)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1≈16.877.
$$

Therefore, the $17$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $10\,000.$

questions.problem: The $4$th term of a geometric sequence with a positive common ratio is $2\,304$, and the $6$th term is $36\,864.$ The first term of this sequence to exceed $496\,800$ is the{{field-1}} th term.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{4}=2\,304$ and ${a}_{6}=36\,864$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{6-4} & =\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{4}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{36\,864}{2\,304} \\ {r}^{2} & =16 \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{4}=2\,304$ and  $r=4$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {4}^{4-1} \\ 2\,304 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {4}^{3} \\ 2\,304 & =64{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =36\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =36\cdot {4}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $496\,800.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}36\cdot {4}^{n-1} & >496\,800 \\ {4}^{n-1} & >13\,800 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({4}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(13\,800) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(4) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(13\,800) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(13\,800)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(13\,800)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(13\,800)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}+1≈7.876.
$$

Therefore, the $8$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $496\,800.$
